rationale: A wins because it does the grown-up PR work: it names which stories can survive and which ones die without proof. Its “The $550 claim: what a flight-deal subscription actually saves” angle is a real money/service story, and the line “Without this, do not pitch this angle at all” is exactly the discipline founders need. B has useful material, especially “The AI travel planner that books nothing,” but it props that up with “the dominant industry narrative” without evidence from the update. That is a fake peg wearing a decent jacket.
gaps_in_A: “a $200 mistake fare” invents a fare price. The update says mistake fare or deep discount, not $200.
“into a booked week” muddies the core fact that no airline or hotel booking happens in-app yet; planning and link-out is the sharper, safer claim.
“Story type: funding-mechanics” is mislabeled. This is a freemium conversion or subscription business-model story, not funding.
“the prevailing assumption is that AI travel tools are racing to own booking” is plausible, but no current-news source was supplied, so it should be framed as a hypothesis, not a peg.
gaps_in_B: “the dominant industry narrative” and “loudly marketed across the industry” are invented context from outside the update. That is how a decent contrarian angle turns into hand-waving.
“category-creation” overclaims the launch. One Premium-only feature does not create a category without competitor evidence or usage data.
It buries the strongest data story. The “$550 average savings per booked flight” methodology deserved its own angle, not just a proof bullet inside the paywall story.
“Resolve real reporter names with journalist-fit-check” is the wrong next step wording. Fit-check vets a journalist once found; it does not build the media list.
